textClass.keywords: Local models Geographically weighted regression Mixed GWR SAR

div.p: Although spatial heterogeneity and spatial dependence are two cornerstones of spatial econometrics, models and methods for dealing at the same time with both issues are still rare in the literature, with few notable exceptions. The same can be said for studies on the performance of spatial econometric models under misspecification of explanatory variables and unknown structure of the spatial weight matrix. In this article, we introduce a new class of data generating processes (DGP), called MGWR-SAR, in which the regression parameters and the spatial autocorrelation coefficient can vary over the space. For the estimation of these new models, we resort to the Spatial Two-Stage Least Squares (S2SLS) technique. We rely on a Monte Carlo experiment for testing the performance of classical models, such as OLS, GWR (Geographically Weighted Regression), mixed GWR and SAR (Spatial AutoRegressive model), as well as our proposals, paying special attention to simulated data under the realistic assumption that they suffer from multicollinearity/concurvity problems and/or misspecification of the covariates. The results suggest that certain model specifications amongst the newly proposed family MGWR-SAR are the more robust. Furthermore, to complete our proposal, we also suggest a specification procedure to identify the correct spatial weight matrix for DGPs with spatial heterogeneity and spatial autocorrelation of the endogenous. We conclude the article with an empirical study on the Lucas County house price dataset, confirming the good performance of the proposed estimators.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Usual spatial-econometric estimation frameworks, based on models with spatial autocorrelation and with a given spatial weight matrix are sometimes unfeasible in the presence of model misspecification. In fact, they are unable to disentangle between real spatial autocorrelation and the different sources of violation of IID, such as non-linear relationship of spatially-correlated independent variables, spatial heterogeneity through unobserved covariates and/or spatially varying relationships (see, amongst others, (Anselin, 1990a;Anselin and Bera, 1998;Brunsdon et al., 1999)). Non-linearities and spatial heterogeneity can cause spatial dependence and the reverse is also true (see, e.g. (Fotheringham, 2009;Pace and LeSage, 2004)) 1 .

Studies that consider both spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity are still scarce in spatial statistics and spatial econo-metrics literature, and even scarcer when possible model misspecification is considered. Tests to diagnose the join presence of spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity, or to test heteroskedasticity taking into account spatial autocorrelation, exist: JLM test of Anselin (1988), KR-SPHET test of Kelejian and Robinson (1998), spatial Breuch-Pagan test, spatial Chow test (Anselin, 1990b), LM test (Mur et al., 2008). However, they are limited to specific forms of spatial variation of the parameters, such as spatial regimes that imply block heteroskedasticity and they are not suitable for more general forms of spatial heterogeneity of model parameters, i.e. when the spatial variation of parameters is continuous (smooth) over the space and depends on coordinates. Moreover, when there is high uncertainty on which spatial interaction matrix to choose or on the model specification, like in the presence of non-linearities and/or unobserved spatial heterogeneity, the existing tests are insufficient for delivering a significant diagnosis of the presence of both spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity of unknown form.

The recent work of Basile et al. (2014) is a nice attempt in this line to promote more flexible estimation frameworks that follow the recommendations of McMillen (2012) of using spatial smoother technics in order to remove spatial heterogeneity while considering other potential non-linearities. The extension of geoadditve models with spatial autocorrelation proposed by Basile et al. (2014) allows to consider spatially autocorelated error terms and/or endogenous variable, and it provides a useful tool for spatial econometrics practitioners.

An alternative to geoadditve models for considering spatiallyvarying coefficients can be found amongst local regression models (Fotheringham et al., 1999;Loader, 1999b;McMillen, 1989): they constitute a simple framework for extending local models in order to account for spatial autocorrelation. For example, Brunsdon et al. (1996) proposed a Spatial AutoRegressive model (a.k.a. SAR) estimated with local maximum likelihood in which all coefficients are spatially varying. Cho et al. (2010) proposed an approach that combines geographically weighted regression (GWR) and Spatial Error Model (SEM), called GWR-SEM, using Generalized Method of Moments (Kelejian and Prucha, 1998). SEM should allay spatial autocorrelation, while GWR addresses spatial heterogeneity by allowing the coefficients to vary across observations. Nevertheless, their model is over-specified, since it has a random intercept term in both the GWR and the SEM part. In the same vein, Páez et al. (2002) propose an estimation method in which the covariance is locally varying and that can handle spatial autocorrelation of the error terms. Another notable contribution accounting for both spatial autocorrelation and non-stationarity of the regression parameters has been made by Pace and LeSage (2004): they propose a spatial autoregressive local estimation based on a recursive approach for maximum-likelihood estimation of SAR that implies estimates on subsamples related to a neighboring of each observation.

The two weaknesses shared by these propositions are that they do not allow to consider the mixed case in which some parameters are constant over space and other are spatially varying and, secondly, that they are computationally intensive. Despite local regression provides a powerful tool to model spatial heterogeneity, it suffers some limitations regarding multicollinearity Barcena et al. (2014); Páez et al. (2017/02); Wheeler and Tiefelsdorf (2005a) and extreme coefficients, including sign reversal Farber and Páez (2007). Particularly, the presence of multicollinearity can lead to artificial spatial patterns of the coefficients, so that other authors prefer to use extended bandwidth Barcena et al. (2014); Páez et al. (2017/02), to use ridge or lasso GWR Wheeler (2007, 2009) or a "mixed" GWR approach, with only a limited number of coefficients that can vary over space. Geniaux et al. (2011) proposed a framework for a specific class of spatial econometrics models in which also the spatial autocorrelation coefficient is non-stationary and the corresponding spatial autoregressive mixed GWR is estimated using local Two-Stage Least Square methods. We show in this paper that the fact that some covariates could be spatially dependent is a key dimension of the problem and that "mixed" GWR approaches are a way of solving the concurvity/multicollinearity problems caused by spatially dependent covariates.

The previous discussion highlights the need for more flexible models where both the regression and the spatial autocorrelation coefficients can either be constant or non-stationary. In Section 2 we provide an economic justification for our approach and we later introduce a set of local regression models that include all possible combinations of constant and spatially-varying coefficients. Each model is presented with its corresponding estimation technique and in Section 3 we present a Monte-Carlo simulation study. The first set of experiments allows to study the finite properties of the proposed estimation techniques, particularly when multi-collinearity/concurvity problems are artificially introduced in the data. In the second set of experiments, each models is estimated over all possible DGPs, with and without misspecification of covariate. In the absence of suitable tests for the joint presence of spatial heterogeneity of general form and spatial dependence, the aim is to asses which model would perform better in case of unknown DGP and is more robust to model misspecification. The last experiment allows to assess the performance of the estimation technique for identifying the spatial weight matrix. Finally, in Section 4, we compare the performance of our proposed methodology against the classical SAR model on the Lucas County pricing data set by comparing their predictive accuracy using cross validation techniques. Conclusions and future developments are sketched in Section 5.

div.head: Spatial econometrics models and estimators with spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity
Motivations for spatially varying coefficient models in urban economics
div.p: Spatial heterogeneity problems in regression models are, in our point of view, inseparable from other issues such as non-linearities and spatial autocorrelation. It is the case, for example, of the effects of land area on land price in hedonic price function estimation: empirical evidence suggests that the relationship between the area and the price of a plot of land is often non-linear, with threshold effects due to zoning regulation (wherever applicable). Furthermore, the spatial distribution of land areas is usually linked to the distance to the city centre, the closer to the city, the smaller the area, but other less-measurable variables can also have an influence on that distribution. Is then easy to prove that not accounting for non-linearities can introduce spatial biases, under the form of spatial autocorrelation and/or unobserved spatial heterogeneity Basile et al. (2014). On the contrary, models that explicitly consider spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity can help reducing the problems of non-linearities Le Gallo (2004). Several authors have also proved that the misspecification of the spatial autocorrelation (either on the form of the model or on the specification of the spatial weight matrix) can introduce spatial heterogeneity and that, on the other hand, considering spatial heterogeneity can reduce the problems issued from spatial autocorrelation. It is then hard to disentangle between spatial autocorrelation, spatial heterogeneity and non-linearities within the calibration of the same model: whenever one of these aspects is ill-specified, it can lead to the creation, intensification or sometimes the disappearance, of the effects of the others. Many authors have discussed the relationship between these three subjects, but, in practice, there is still no clear agreement and the vast majority of spatial econometric practitioners still resort to classical models that only consider spatial autocorrelation. We then highlight that the interest in regression models with spatial heterogeneity has not been sufficiently promoted and justified from the economic point of view, as well as the importance of considering spatial heterogeneity, spatial autocorrelation and non-linearity jointly. The interest in using regression models with spatially-varying coefficients is then multiple. Firstly, we can argue that models that only consider spatial autocorrelation are not capable of correcting all the problems related to non-observable spatial heterogeneity. This has pushed several authors to consider a non-stationary intercept term amongst the regression variables, for example, by means of a spline function of the space coordinates Wood (2011). Nonetheless, this same argument can be pushed even further to consider a regression model with more spatially-varying coefficients. To keep the example of hedonic price function of land sales, it is sometimes difficult to have access to detailed urban regulation; these unobserved variables can sometimes introduce spatial heterogeneity that can only be partially taken into account by SEM models or models with a spatially-varying intercept term. The resultant of these variables cannot be accounted as either a fixed or a random effect in reduced form of micro-econometric models, but it should rather be understood as an indicator of a different economic behaviour, hence it demands a differentiation of the parameters of agent preferences (indirect utility function) that drives bidding process. Similarly, Brady and Irwin (2011) invoked this same argument to promote the use of models that integrate spatial heterogeneity in order to better account for the variability of willingness to pay with respect to environmental amenities, according to socio-spatial segregation of individuals: they affirm that the propensity of householders for green or open spaces can vary according to their socio-professional category or their level of revenue that, on the other hand, are often clustered in space. Likewise, the willingness to pay of individuals for parking lots can vary strongly over the space according, for example, to urban density, type of neighborhood or proximity to public transportation. These two examples fit better in the logic of a model with spatial differentiation of the regressors rather than with spatial interaction.

The choice of a model with spatial autocorrelation, justified merely as a microeconomic model with agents interactions (see (Brueckner, 2006)), is just a way to include a spatial structure to the specification and to allow the evaluation of the marginal effects. Nonetheless, the same can be achieved by means of other statistical methods that can include spatially-varying coefficients (McMillen, 2004(McMillen, , 2010)). Another way of justifying this approach is to write explicitly the underlying micro-economic model in which some variables of the price function depend on some unobserved spatial covariates. For example, Geniaux et al. (2011) have applied an inter-temporal utility model for land price with non-stationary coefficients to evaluate the anticipation of land owners on the likelihood of future development of their lands: the level of anticipation varied over the space according to stability/uncertainty of land regulation in the neighborhood which is not directly observable.

In our propositions, we also consider the possibility of a nonstationary spatial autocorrelation parameter. This possibility is based on its theoretical soundness, even if some economic behavior can be evoked to justify it: when the spatial weight matrix W is unknown and spatial locations are irregularly distributed over space, the choice of a neighboring scheme based only on distance or first nearest neighbours can be tricky. Choosing one weighting scheme instead of the other can lead to a spatial interaction matrix that is too dense (resp. too dispersed) in the heterogeneous parts of the space, resulting in under or overestimation of the spatial parameter. There exist at least two possible solutions to mitigate the effect of the spatial weight matrix misspecification with cross section data: either to adapt the structure of W in order to improve the quality of the fit ( (Ertur and Koch, 2006;Meen, 1996;Mur et al., 2008), see Section 2.3.4) keeping a stationary spatial parameter or to use of a non-stationary spatial autocorrelation parameter like in our proposition. This highlight the link between a suitable choice of W when considering both spatial autocorrelation and spatial dependence, so we also propose in Section 2.3.4 a method for choosing W in such settings.

div.head: Estimators for models with spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity
div.p: Although most of the models involving local parameters are unidentifiable because they suppose more parameters than observations, we found in the literature different ways to approximate these local coefficients by introducing conditions on local continuity and smoothness. The first approach in this field consisted in parametric models incorporating the spatial coordinates of observations as for example the "Trend Surface Analysis" method Ripley (2005) or "Variable Expansion" method proposed by Casetti (1972Casetti ( , 1997)). Nevertheless, while these parametric methods allowed to identify a spatial trend valid throughout the sample, they were unable to detect local variations Fotheringham et al. (1999). After that, the main contributions considered semi-parametric methods like the "Locally Weighted Regression" (LWR) McMillen (1996) and the "Geographically Weighted Regression" (GWR) Brunsdon et al. (1996) who provided a methodological framework to estimate local values of the parameters from local regressions. The idea was to estimate as many regressions as focal points (data coordinates or other sets of coordinates) by weighting the local regressions with respect to the observations' distance to these focal points. The Mixed GWR introduced by Fotheringham et al. (1999) and extended by Mei et al. (2004) and Geniaux et al. (2011) allows to combine spatially stationary and non-stationary coefficients.

A notable contribution that takes into account the spatial autocorrelation in a local regression framework has been made by Pace and LeSage (2004). They proposed a "Spatial Autoregressive Local Estimation" based on a recursive approach for maximum-likelihood estimation of SAR, implying estimates on subsamples related to a neighboring of each observation. Despite the fact that they used local estimates of the spatial parameter, they did not really exploited that possibility and only focused on the spatial variability of the parameter β. Moreover, their proposition did not allow to consider the mixed-GWR case and it was computationally very intensive.

Amongst the DGPs that implies both spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity, the MGWR-SAR( k 1, 0, ) has been studied in the spatial econometric literature Fotheringham et al. (1999); Páez et al. (2002) (known there as simply "mixed GWR"). The MGWR-SAR( k 1, , 0) model was already introduced in Brunsdon et al. (1998). While these authors proposed local maximum likelihood estimation, if we want to rely only on linear regression to keep reasonable computation time, the parameters of such DGP should be estimated using the "Spatial Two-Stage Least Squares" (S2SLS) Anselin (1988); Kelejian and Prucha (1998). We also explored another estimation technique, notably the "Best Spatial Two-Stage Least Squares" (BS2SLS) of Lee Lee (2003), that can be relevant here in case of misspecification of the true model DGP but the results were not convincing and are not presented in this version of the paper (although they are available upon request).

All the estimators and methods proposed in the following sections have been coded in C++ and embedded into R through the Rcpp package Eddelbuettel et al. (2011). They are the core functions of a forthcoming R package, called gwrsar.

div.p: Another issue concerning bandwidth selection is related to models with spatially-varying λ estimated via S2SLS. For such models, the S2SLS method could lead to an estimation of λ that is out of the domain interval [-1, 1] for those bandwidths h that are too small. To avoid such issue, we use a penalized CV criteria with an arbitrary large penalty for bandwidth values that lead to an out-of-support λ. The chosen kernel will be the one showing the smallest penalized CV criteria.

In search of W . As suggested in Section 2.1, the issue of estimating λ ij presents several analogies with the estimation procedures that propose to adapt the structure of W by iteratively modifying w ij to improve the fit Bhattacharjee and Jensen-Butler (2006); Ertur and Koch (2006); Jennrich (2001); Meen (1996); Mur et al. (2008). A choice of W that corresponds to the true data generating process is then crucial, since otherwise we will observe dramatic changes of parameter estimates and explanatory variables specification Bhattacharjee and Jensen-Butler (2006). Harris et al. (2011) identified three main approaches for choosing W. First, it is common practice to compare pre-specified versions of W using "goodness of fit statistics", like AIC, to choose the best specification of W. LeSage and Fischer (2008) use Bayesian technics for choosing between non-nested competing models, while Stakhovych and Bijmolt (2009) show through Monte Carlo experiments that information criteria could also be a valid option for choosing W. However, such approaches provide a local maximum for which substantial bias of regression estimates may still remain. A second approach starts with an unspecified spatial weight matrix W and try to fit it in such a way that it is consistent with observed patterns of spatial dependence. Conley (1999) proposes a method to estimate the spatial auto-covariance matrix involving imperfect measures of economic distance. In the same vain, Pinkse et al. (2002) develop a framework with uncertainty on distance measures and the possibility of spatial non-stationarity. Mur et al. (2008) proposed the zoom estimation based on local ML estimates that adapt the number of neighbors to consider in W for each observation. When observations over time are available, the original proposal of Meen (1996) has been extended by Beenstock and Felsenstein (2012); Bhattacharjee and Jensen-Butler (2006); Harris et al. (2011)to construct W by taking benefits of the panel structure of the data, without requiring the pre-specification of W when N is small, relative to T (time). Finally, a third approach is to use non parametric approaches for measuring spatial correlation of a single variable. For example, López et al. (2010) use the concept of symbolic entropy as a measure of spatial dependence, while other authors propose the use of Moran I (see (Ord and Getis, 1995)) or local statistics (see (Aldstadt and Getis, 2006)) to identify the most suitable W.

Our proposal is to use a parametric approach that is at the frontier of the approaches discussed earlier. The estimation procedure uses a family of distance kernels with a single parameter h w (the bandwidth or the number of neighbors, according to the kernel). To identify the matrix W, we use a moment estimator that tries to minimize the residual sum of squares (RSS) of the model estimation with respect to W h ( ) w . In this paper, we consider only three types of kernel: k-nearest neighbors with rectangular kernel, bisquare or adaptive bisquare. The search is performed for each kernel, in order to find the best value of h w . The final choice correspond to the pair of kernel/bandwidth that assures the best RSS for the model.

div.head: Monte Carlo experiments
div.p: In this section we present three Monte Carlo experiments. The first set of experiments focuses on the finite properties of the proposed estimation techniques, particularly when multi-collinearity/concurvity problems are artificially introduced in the simulated data. In the second set of experiments, each models is estimated over all possible DGPs, with and without misspecification of covariates, to assess the robustness of the estimators. The last experiment allows to assess the performance of the estimation technique for finding the right specification of W.

When simulating data with spatial heterogeneity, our three Monte Carlo experiments consider always DGPs in which all coefficients are non-stationary. div.head: Experiment 1: multicollinearity/concurvity problems
div.p: Before testing our family of estimators (MGWR-SAR), we first focus on the potential sources of bias estimation when the data are analyzed via a standard GWR model. To do that, we simulate different datasets, where the introduction of a spatially dependent variable X 2 leads to concurvity problems between the β u v ( ,

div.p: This problem has been already partially addressed for GWR estimators through collinearity analysis of certain variables in local samples Páez et al. (2017/02); Wheeler and Tiefelsdorf (2005b), but it makes the estimation of the parameters not reliable. For example, Wheeler (2007Wheeler ( , 2009) ) proposed to use ridge or LASSO GWR, while Brunsdon et al. (2012) and Barcena et al. (2014) used "extended kernels" (whenever collinearity is detected, the kernel extends to consider a bigger local neighbourhood). On the other hand, Páez et al. (2017/02) and Fotheringham and Oshan (2016) showed that using sufficiently large local samples in the GWR could improve the quality of the estimated parameters. Nevertheless, the finite-sample properties of estimators adopting these strategies have only been studied on simulated data where all variables where generated 2 The MGWR-SAR( k 1, , 0 c ) DGP has not been included because it can be considered as a special case of the MGWR-SAR( k k 1, , c v).

In order to correct for the bias introduced by the spatially dependent variable X 2 , we test the performance of mixed models (MGWR) with different combinations of fixed and spatially varying coefficients (again on data generated with a GWR DGP and spatially dependent X 2 ). We immediately observe in Table 2 that the introduction of fixed coefficients reduce the bias relative to the coefficients β 0 and β 2 . Notably, fixing β 2 reduces by one half the bias, while fixing the intercept or the intercept and β 2 , leads to more significant improvements. In some sense, fixing these coefficients coincides conceptually with the idea of using extended kernels Brunsdon et al. (2012); Barcena et al. (2014): if we take the kernel extension to the extremes, we enlarge the local sample up to cover the entire space. Nonetheless, in contrast with the proposition of these authors, we only extend the parameters that correspond to the problematic variables.

To conclude the first experiment we also consider the case of DGPs with spatially varying coefficients and spatial autocorrelation of the dependent variable, with the λ coefficient either fixed (MGWR-SAR(0,0,4)) or spatially varying (MGWR-SAR(1,0,4)). div.head: Experiment 2: robustness of MGWR-SAR estimators
div.p: The first experiment taught us that it is preferable to use mixed models whenever we detect that certain independent variables are spatially dependent, and that the coefficients corresponding to those variables and the intercept should be kept stationary. In empirical studies, we suggest to test spatial autocorrelation of all covariates in order to detect potentially problematic variables. It is worth noting that the problems of identification of the parameters for the GWR, MGWR-SAR( k 0, 0, v ) and MGWR- SAR( k 1, 0, v ) models makes complicated the use of asymptotic tests Leung et al. (2000); Páez et al. (2002); Wei and Qi (2012) for the identification of the true DGP, even in case of applying a correction adapted to the critical thresholds as a function of the d.o.f. Páez et al. (2002). Alternatively, bootstrap tests like the one proposed by Mei et al. (2016) can contribute to the identification of the stationary coefficients.

div.p: In the second experiment we focus on the robustness of the different estimators w.r.t. unknown DGP. Such experiment is indispensable, since there exist no test in the literature that is capable of detecting simultaneously spatially heterogeneity and spatial dependence, hence there is no way of choosing the model specification based on solid assumptions. Since we plan to cross different DGP and estimators, there is no point in looking at the bias of the estimators parameters and we rather turn to the bias of marginal spatial effects. For example, if the true DGP is a SAR model and we use a OLS for the estimation, we are more interested in the ability of the OLS of approximating I λW β ( -) -1 , instead that a comparison against the initial parameters that does not account for the predictive capability of the estimator. From Tables 5678, in which the darker shades of grey indicates the smallest BIAS/RMSE and the lighter shades of grey indicates the second best, we can observe that:
• the most severe bias are again on the parameters β 0 and β 2 ; • OLS estimates are always biased as far as spatial heterogeneity or spatial autocorrelation are introduced in the DGP;
• MGWR estimates are always biased as far as spatial autocorrelation are introduced in the DGP;

• the MGWR-SAR(0,2,2) estimator with stationary β 0 and β 2 seems to be the more robust, since it is always the first or second best performing, independently on the true DGP, and it allows to avoid too high biases in the presence of spatial heterogeneity and/or spatial autocorrelation.

If we introduce misspecification on the variable X 2 (Table 9), we observe that both bias and RMSE tend to increase, while the hierarchy of best estimators remains the same, except for the case of SAR DGP where the estimation of λ is biased and it makes models without spatial autocorrelation (OLS and MGWR) preferable. This is in line with what observed in Le Gallo and Fingleton (2012), where OLS estimators prove better performance than standard techniques, in the context of spatial models with measurement errors of the independent variable. Similar conclusion can be reached for the case of an increase of the signal-to-noise ratio (see (Kelley Pace et al., 2012), Eq. ( 62)) that makes models with spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity (MGWR-SAR(0,2,2) and MGWR-SAR(1,2,2)) preferable. Whenever the expected adjustment of the model is poor, due to an increase of σ and/or of the misspecification on the variable X 2 , we observe that the MGWR-SAR(0,2,2) and MGWR-SAR(1,2,2) estimators are no longer the second best choice. Instead, it appears more important the ability to test if spatial heterogeneity and or spatial autocorrelation are present. Nonetheless, both MGWR-SAR(0,2,2) and MGWR-SAR(1,2,2) remain at a reasonable distance from the best performing model and still insure to avoid too high bias. The take-home message from the second experiment is then the following: the more robust estimators in case of lack of appropriate tests for model specification that encompass all DGPs considered here, are MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) and MGWR-SAR( k k 1, , c v ) (Table 10).

For the three DGPs with spatial autocorrelation used in the second experiment, we compute the percentage of correct identification according to the following criteria:
• the kernel is correctly identified and • the estimated bandwidth is less than 5% apart from the true bandwidth used for generating the true W.

div.head: Empirical study on Lucas county pricing data
div.p: We conclude the experimentations of the proposed MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) method and the W-identification procedure by testing their performance on a real data set. We consider the well-known Lucas county house-price datasetfoot_1 , in line with what has been done by other authors such as LeSage and Pace (2009); Bivand (2010) and Basile et al. (2014), when treating with comparable spatial issues.
We plan to test the following models:
• SAR model with W soi as in Basile et al. (2014);
• SAR model with W opt issued from our identification procedure; • MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) with W opt issued from our identification procedure.

In Table 12, we present the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS), the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Predicted Mean Square Error for two train/test splitting strategies (PMSE 10 for 10-fold cross validation and PMSE 20 for 20-fold cross validation, see Shao (1993)). For the latter, PMSE 10 and PMSE 20 , the predictions on the out-of-sample data have been computed by means of the Best Linear Unbiased Predictor (BLUP)foot_2 , that ensure a better performance than using directly the parameters estimated on the in-sample data. The first observation concerns the choice of the spatial weight matrix W: the matrix W soi is computed from a sphere-of-influence (soi) graph constructed from a triangulation of the point coordinates of the houses after projection to the Ohio North NAD83 Lambert Conformal Conical specification. The resulting matrix is relatively sparse, with less than three neighbors per observation Basile et al. (2014). On the other hand, the matrix W opt chosen by our identification algorithm is constructed with an adaptive kernel with 12 nearest neighbors (see Eq. ( 9)), where closest observations are assigned higher weights. Actually, we can observe that the first three neighbours (out of 12) of each observation in W opt absorb almost 40% of the total weight for that observation, meaning that W soi and W opt are, in principle, comparable.

By comparing the results of the SAR estimation with W soi and W opt , we notice that the estimation with W opt is always better (in terms of both RSS and AIC) than the one with (W soi )foot_3 . In conclusion, we can say that the predictive power of the two methods is comparable, but that our approach can be considered as an "off-the-shelf" solution that does not requires to make assumptions on the true form of the spatial weight.

For the MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) estimator, the first issue is choosing the parameters that will be spatially stationary. The variable ''baths" is almost an obligate choice, since discrete variables are very likely to create problems in local samples. Since all the other continuous variables are spatially dependentfoot_4 , we chose to test the out-of-sample predictive power for all combinations of spatially stationary and nonstationary. Based on this criteria, we finally retained the intercept, the number of bathrooms and the (log of the) lot size as spatially stationary variables, while age and (log of the) total living area are spatially nonstationary.

The performance of the MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) model improves considerably that of the SAR specification, in terms of RSS, AIC and PMSE. Nonetheless, the remarkable drop of the RSS of the MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) model should be put into perspective, accounting for the fact that this model has different degrees of freedom. On the other hand, both AIC, PMSE 10 and PMSE 20 criteria allow a direct comparison of the MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) against the SAR model: we then observe that the decrease is substantial and favors the mixed model. Results for PMSE 10 and PMSE 20 are similar and highlight the good performance of MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) model: the PMSE 10 decreases between 10% and 18% according to the year. We think that a 15% mean improvement in the predictive power of a model that has already been the subject of several researches is undoubtedly an encouraging result and proves once more the advantage of having more flexible models: in empirical situations, where the true DGP and W are unknown, the possibility of adjusting the structure of the spatial weight matrix and of choosing amongst different combination of stationary and non-stationary parameters, can help reducing the unsolvable identification problem of empirical spatial data. div.head: Conclusions and future works
div.p: The goal of this paper was to study the problem of spatial regression models with spatial autocorrelation of the dependent variable and spatial heterogeneity of the parameters, a subject that has not received enough attention in the literature, but that it is crucial for spatial econometric practitioners. In Section 2.2 we recalled existing techniques to deal with either spatial autocorrelation of the dependent variable (SAR model) or spatial heterogeneity of the regression parameters (GWR model if all coefficients vary over the space or MGWR if some coefficients are stationary and others are not). We also proposed four new models that simultaneously accounts for both autocorrelation of the endogenous variable and spatial heterogeneity of the parameters.

These models are more flexible, since they relax the hypothesis on the nature of the spatial interactions. The results of a series of Monte Carlo experiments show that they are also more robust to certain types of misspecification of the model. In particular, it appeared that mixed models with a combination of stationary and non-stationary regression coefficients are more reliable, since they reduce identification problems. In fact, MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ) and MGWR-SAR( k k 1, , c v ) models are often amongst the best or the second best, especially when faced to the presence of autocorrelation of the endogenous variable and spatial heterogeneity of the regression coefficients.

Another issue that arose during the Monte Carlo experiments is that the presence of spatially dependent covariates have a strong impact on the performance of certain models. In fact, we included in the DGPs a variable which value is dependent on its location and that caused different models, especially those with non-stationary coefficients, to underperform w.r.t. the case of non-spatially dependent covariates. Although there exist tests for the detection of spatial dependence, we found that specification tests in the literature never consider the case of a DGP with spatially dependent regressors. In view of the results of our experiment, we foster the study of appropriate tests that also consider spatially dependent covariates, while the use of bootstrap tests can provide a first solution, whenever the sample size and the number covariates remain treatable.

Regarding the choice of stationary and non-stationary coefficients, it seems that good performances are achieved by leaving only the intercept term amongst the stationary coefficients. Further improvements can be obtained by adding some of those coefficients that correspond to spatially dependent covariates to the set of stationary coefficients. Indeed, in empirical settings, we are likely to find a large number of strongly spatially-dependent regressors, and some of them can generate more or less concurvity problems than others: as rule of thumb, our results suggest that out-of-sample cross-validation procedures should be prioritized for choosing the set of spatially varying coefficients.

We also tested a specification procedure for the identification of the spatial weight matrix W. The results on the accuracy of the identification procedure on simulated data are very encouraging. Furthermore when we applied this strategy to the Lucas dataset using a SAR model, we have been able to slightly improve the results with respect to the SAR estimation with the original W matrix.

In order to improve the performance of our model specification procedure, that is burdened by an high number of iterations over several different DGPs and possible specifications of the spatial structure, we see the urgent need for asymptotic tests for:
• non-stationarity of the spatial autocorrelation parameter (in our notation, MGWR-SAR(0, •,•) vs. MGWR-SAR(1, •,•));
• detecting spatial autocorrelation for mixed models (MGWR vs MGWR-SAR( k k 0, , c v ));
• identifying mixed vs non-mixed models in the presence of spatial autocorrelation (MGWR-SAR( k 0, 0, ) vs. MGWR-SAR( k k 0, ,

In our contribution, scarce attention has been paid to the estimation time required by the different methods. Nevertheless, in the future we will look for improved estimators, capable of handling large samples in reasonable time. For this purpose, we plan to use the target-point technique for the family of MGWR-SAR models as already proposed by Loader (1999a) for regression models and by McMillen and Redfearn (2010); McMillen (2012) for the GWR model. Other proposals for improving the computational efficiency of the estimators are to use the Estimated Generalized Least Squares (EGLS) and Maximum Likelihood methods proposed by Pace and Barry (1997a), provided that we can extend these techniques to the MGWR-SAR family of models. Finally, the exponential matrix model proposed by LeSage and Pace (2007) can also be used to reduce computational requirements: this method implies the transformation of the spatial weight matrix inverse by means of the so called matrix exponential. This allow to avoid the computation of log-determinant of large matrices.
